title: 1 Chronicles 18:1–8
context: 1 Chronicles 18 parallels 2 Samuel 8 and follows the covenant promise of chapter 17, showing God subduing David’s enemies (17:10). David defeats the Philistines, Moab, Hadadezer of Zobah, and the Syrians of Damascus, hamstrings the chariot horses, and brings gold and bronze to Jerusalem; the Chronicler adds that Solomon later used the bronze for the temple. Chronicles differs from 2 Samuel 8 in some names, numbers, and details, which the notes name without trying to resolve. The refrain “The LORD gave victory to David wherever he went” frames the account. Both traditions read it as shared ground about God’s faithfulness to his promise.

verses.text: After this, David defeated the Philistines and subdued them, and took Gath and its towns out of the hand of the Philistines.
verses.arminianNotes:
David defeats and subdues the Philistines and takes Gath and its towns from them. The long Philistine threat is broken.

Arminian readers see God’s promise to subdue David’s enemies (17:10) beginning to be realized.
verses.reformedNotes:
Where Chronicles names Gath and its towns, 2 Samuel 8:1 speaks of “the bridle of the mother city.” The text does not explain the difference.

Reformed readers see God fulfilling his word. Both traditions read this as shared ground and leave the difference unresolved.

verses.text: He defeated Moab; and the Moabites became servants to David and brought tribute.
verses.arminianNotes:
David defeats Moab, and the Moabites become his servants and bring tribute. The report is brief.

Arminian readers see Moab brought under David’s rule as part of the summary of his victories.
verses.reformedNotes:
Chronicles does not include the measuring of Moabite captives with a line recorded in 2 Samuel 8:2, which the 2 Samuel notes read soberly.

Reformed readers see God extending David’s rule. Both traditions read this as shared ground and do not speculate on the omission.

verses.text: David defeated Hadadezer king of Zobah, toward Hamath, as he went to establish his dominion by the river Euphrates.
verses.arminianNotes:
David defeats Hadadezer king of Zobah, toward Hamath, as he goes to establish his dominion by the river Euphrates. The campaign reaches far north.

Arminian readers see Israel’s influence extending toward the bounds promised to Abraham.
verses.reformedNotes:
Chronicles names the Euphrates and Hamath; 2 Samuel 8:3 says “at the River” and names Hadadezer as son of Rehob. Whose dominion is meant is not certain.

Reformed readers see ancient promises advancing. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: David took from him one thousand chariots, seven thousand horsemen, and twenty thousand footmen; and David hamstrung all the chariot horses, but reserved of them enough for one hundred chariots.
verses.arminianNotes:
David takes one thousand chariots, seven thousand horsemen, and twenty thousand footmen, and hamstrings all the chariot horses but keeps enough for one hundred chariots. The text gives no comment.

Arminian readers read the act plainly in its own setting.
verses.reformedNotes:
2 Samuel 8:4 reads one thousand seven hundred horsemen and twenty thousand footmen, with no thousand chariots. The difference is noted, not resolved; the 2 Samuel 8:4 notes discuss the hamstringing.

Reformed readers likewise read the act soberly in its setting. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: When the Syrians of Damascus came to help Hadadezer king of Zobah, David struck twenty-two thousand men of the Syrians.
verses.arminianNotes:
When the Syrians of Damascus come to help Hadadezer, David strikes twenty-two thousand of them. The coalition fails.

Arminian readers see David’s victories continuing as other nations ally against him.
verses.reformedNotes:
The number matches 2 Samuel 8:5. The intervention only widens David’s success.

Reformed readers see God’s promise to subdue David’s enemies being kept. Both traditions read this as shared ground, part of the summary of victories that the Chronicler presents as God’s gift to David.

verses.text: Then David put garrisons in Syria of Damascus; and the Syrians became servants to David and brought tribute. The LORD gave victory to David wherever he went.
verses.arminianNotes:
David places garrisons in Syria of Damascus, and the Syrians become his servants and bring tribute. The LORD gives victory to David wherever he goes.

Arminian readers see success credited to the LORD rather than to David’s skill alone.
verses.reformedNotes:
The refrain, repeated at 18:13, matches 2 Samuel 8:6 and 8:14 and frames the chapter theologically.

Reformed readers see victory belonging to the LORD. Both traditions read this as clear shared ground.

verses.text: David took the shields of gold that were on the servants of Hadadezer, and brought them to Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes:
David takes the gold shields carried by Hadadezer’s servants and brings them to Jerusalem. The spoils come to the capital.

Arminian readers see wealth and honor coming to Jerusalem under God’s blessing, as the parallel in 2 Samuel 8:7 also records.
verses.reformedNotes:
The gold shields join the other spoils that David will dedicate to the LORD in verse 11.

Reformed readers see Jerusalem becoming the center of God’s kingdom. Both traditions read this as shared ground and find no doctrinal question in it.

verses.text: From Tibhath and from Cun, cities of Hadadezer, David took very much bronze, with which Solomon made the bronze sea, the pillars, and the vessels of bronze.
verses.arminianNotes:
From Tibhath and Cun, cities of Hadadezer, David takes much bronze, which Solomon later uses for the bronze sea, the pillars, and the bronze vessels. Victory serves the future temple.

Arminian readers see David’s gains devoted to worship.
verses.reformedNotes:
2 Samuel 8:8 names the cities Betah and Berothai and does not mention Solomon’s use of the bronze. The difference is noted, not resolved.

Reformed readers see the temple promised in 17:12 being prepared. Both traditions read this as shared ground.
